stem: A 52-year-old patient with stable chronic plaque psoriasis has been well-controlled on topical therapy. Recently, the patient was started on a new medication for hypertension. Over the next few weeks, the psoriasis lesions worsen, with increased erythema and scaling. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible?
stemHtml: Q 09: A 52-year-old patient with stable chronic plaque psoriasis has been well-controlled on topical therapy. Recently, the patient was started on a new medication for hypertension. Over the next few weeks, the psoriasis lesions worsen, with increased erythema and scaling. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible? (Question Id: 515025)
keywords: “Worsening of psoriasis lesions” – Indicates drug-induced exacerbation of chronic plaque psoriasis.
“Started on a new medication for hypertension” – Suggests the trigger is a cardiovascular drug recently initiated.
“Over the next few weeks” – Highlights the temporal relationship between drug initiation and psoriasis flare.
keywordsHtml: 1. “Worsening of psoriasis lesions” – Indicates drug-induced exacerbation of chronic plaque psoriasis.

1. “Over the next few weeks” – Highlights the temporal relationship between drug initiation and psoriasis flare.

E.title: Beta-blocker
E.body:
Beta-blockers are well-known to exacerbate or trigger psoriasis in susceptible individuals.
Mechanism: When these receptors are blocked, there is a decrease in intracellular cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) levels. Lower cAMP levels lead to increased keratinocyte proliferation and a decrease in differentiation, which directly fuels the formation of the thick, scaly plaques characteristic of psoriasis. This reaction can occur weeks or even months after starting the medication.
Timing: usually weeks after initiation, as described in the case.

A.title: ACE inhibitor
A.body:
Rarely associated with drug-induced psoriasis.
More commonly linked to angioedema, cough, hyperkalemia.
Less likely the culprit in psoriasis flare.
A.bodyHtml:
• Rarely associated with drug-induced psoriasis.
  • More commonly linked to angioedema, cough, hyperkalemia.
  • Less likely the culprit in psoriasis flare.

B.title: Calcium channel blocker
B.body:
Generally safe regarding psoriasis.
Main adverse effects: edema, hypotension, bradycardia.
Not commonly implicated in worsening psoriasis.
B.bodyHtml:
• Generally safe regarding psoriasis.
  • Main adverse effects: edema, hypotension, bradycardia.
  • Not commonly implicated in worsening psoriasis.

C.title: Thiazide diuretic
C.body:
Can cause photosensitivity, electrolyte disturbances, and sometimes skin rashes.
Psoriasis exacerbation is uncommon.
C.bodyHtml:
• Can cause photosensitivity, electrolyte disturbances, and sometimes skin rashes.
  • Psoriasis exacerbation is uncommon.

D.title: Statin
D.body:
Mostly used for dyslipidemia.
Can rarely cause skin reactions like rash or pruritus, but psoriasis worsening is not typical.
D.bodyHtml:
• Mostly used for dyslipidemia.
  • Can rarely cause skin reactions like rash or pruritus, but psoriasis worsening is not typical.

keyConcept: Beta-blockers are a common cause of drug-induced psoriasis exacerbation. When psoriasis worsens after starting a new medication, especially for cardiovascular conditions, always consider beta-blockers first. Recognizing drug triggers is important for dermatologic and systemic management.

diagram.name: Drug-Induced Exacerbation of Psoriasis
diagram.caption: The diagram illustrates how certain medications, particularly beta-blockers, can trigger worsening of pre-existing plaque psoriasis. It shows a patient with flaring skin lesions and highlights the pathophysiology: increased inflammation and keratinocyte overgrowth. The flow emphasizes the temporal link between new drug initiation and lesion exacerbation, key clinical clues (recent drug change, timing), and management strategies (discontinue offending drug, adjust psoriasis therapy).
